title: The training principles series: full range of motion
summary: NH explains that range of motion depends on leverages and that 'full' ROM standards are subjective conventions mainly useful for judging strength sports. For bodybuilding, full ROM stretches the muscle more and prepares you for deep reps, so do it about 80% of the time, but partials have a place if chosen for gains, not ego. Avoid excessive ROM (hyperextending curls, butt wink) and adapt deadlift start height if needed.

claims.claim: Range of motion is the distance the weight travels and depends on individual leverages (arm, forearm, humerus, leg proportions), so it isn't absolute.
Full-ROM standards are 100% subjective conventions: on bench, a cambered bar or dumbbells would allow even more range than chest-to-lockout.
Dumbbell bench usually ends up with less ROM than barbell in practice because the dumbbells hit the chest.
Fixed ROM standards exist mainly to judge strength sports like powerlifting, where lifters still find ways to cut ROM within the rules.
Bodybuilders aren't tested on strength, so ROM standards matter less as a measure; full ROM matters because a muscle worked through full range stretches more and grows more.
Always training a shortened ROM may leave gains on the table and make you injury-prone: a quarter-squatter who accidentally goes deep isn't prepared for it. Train full ROM at least at some point.
He never locks out his elbows on presses because it removes triceps tension and destroys his elbows; if locking knees on squats hurts, don't do it.
On the deadlift, lock knees, hips and shoulders at the top to finish standing straight, then reset; it's the strongest aligned position and rarely causes pain.
Full ROM is best for hypertrophy: the muscle travels farther, is stretched and under tension longer, both through the stretch and the concentric.
If you shorten ROM, know why: 'I can lift more weight' is not a valid bodybuilder answer; 'I get better gains from it' is.
Partial ROM work can help you get stronger on the full-ROM lift.
Do full range of motion about 80% of the time; partials have their place.

There is such a thing as too much ROM: fully hyperextending the elbow at the bottom of a curl loads the tendons once the biceps is maximally lengthened, risking biceps tears. Stay within the range where the muscle is active.
If you get a big pelvic tilt (butt wink) at the bottom of an ass-to-grass squat, cut the depth: watch in the mirror and push up as soon as the butt starts tucking under.
He disagrees with videos claiming butt wink isn't dangerous: it contributes to lumbar rounding and back injury risk.
Almost everyone should find some stance (sumo, Jefferson, conventional) to pull safely from the floor.
Deadlift ROM is also fabricated by using 45 lb plate diameter; if you truly can't pull from the floor safely, pull from blocks; that becomes your full ROM.
ROM is plagued by dogmatism; 'full range or don't lift' is elitist. Lift within a comfortable range, push mobility safely, and combine full ROM with partials for more gains.

exercises.name: Bench press
cues: bar to chest, but he doesn't fully lock out elbows
exercises.why: keeps triceps tension and protects elbows

exercises.name: Dumbbell bench press
exercises.why: theoretically more ROM; limited by dumbbells touching chest

exercises.name: Squat
cues: stop and push up as soon as the butt starts tucking under (butt wink)
don't lock knees if it hurts

exercises.name: Deadlift
cues: lock knees, hips and shoulders at the top
pull from blocks if floor is unsafe

exercises.name: Biceps curl
cues: don't hyperextend the elbow at the bottom
stay where the muscle, not the tendon, is stretched
